claims.text: Superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys is governed primarily by atomic-disorder-induced electron scattering.
Disorder-induced electron scattering enhances electron pairing by modifying the density of states at the Fermi level.
The as-cast high-entropy alloy has a high degree of random atomic distribution.
Controlled thermal annealing can partially order the alloy and reduce atomic disorder without changing its overall elemental composition.
Annealing can be controlled such that the degree of atomic disorder is the only materially changed variable and no mechanical stress is added.
The degree of chemical disorder can be quantified using local atomic-arrangement metrics obtained from X-ray diffraction or electron microscopy.
Greater atomic disorder increases the electron-scattering rate.
Increased electron scattering enhances the density of states near the Fermi level.
An enhanced density of states near the Fermi level facilitates Cooper-pair formation.
Reducing disorder through annealing lowers the electron-scattering rate.
A lower electron-scattering rate causes a reduction in the superconducting transition temperature.
The highly disordered as-cast sample will have a higher superconducting transition temperature than the compositionally identical, partially ordered annealed sample.
The proposed disorder mechanism is significant only when chemical complexity is sufficiently high to produce notable atomic disorder.
In lower-entropy or inherently more ordered alloys, factors such as phonon coupling may dominate superconducting behavior.
Annealing-related changes in electron-phonon coupling may also affect the superconducting transition temperature.

Failure to observe a significant decrease in transition temperature or a correlation between disorder and transition temperature would falsify the proposed governing role of disorder-induced scattering.
